title: Ohio Teen Owen Gee Commits to Texas A&M Swimming for 2028
summary:
Owen Gee, a high school swimmer from Morrow, Ohio, has announced his verbal commitment to continue his academic and athletic career at Texas A&M University. He's a "Best of the Rest" ranked recruit for the boys high school class of 2028.

"I am honored and thankful to announce my commitment to continue my athletic and academic career at Texas A&M!" Gee wrote. He thanked his family, Coach Brandon, his teammates, and the Texas A&M coaching staff — including Coaches Blaire and Wes — for "believing in me and giving me this amazing opportunity." Then he added the school's famous cheer: "Gig 'Em!"

Gee swims for the Cincinnati Marlins and St. Xavier High School. At Summer Juniors, he swam numerous lifetime bests. His highest finish was 6th in the 200 butterfly with a time of 2:01.80, and he went even faster in prelims — 2:01.18 — to place 4th. He also posted lifetime bests in the 100 fly (54.23), 50 fly (24.90), and 100 free (51.42).

Back in February, swimming for St. Xavier, he finished 3rd in the 100 fly at the Ohio Division I State Championships with a 48.35. He was also 2nd in the 500 free (4:34.84) and led off his team's winning 400 free relay in a lifetime best 45.90.

Based on his best times, Gee would have been 6th in the 200 fly and 8th in the 100 fly on Texas A&M's roster this past season. For comparison, Chase Swearingen led the Aggies with a 45.30 100 fly, while Alejandro Michelena led the team with a 1:41.96 200 fly. It took a 46.48 100 fly and a 1:44.80 200 fly just to final at the 2026 SEC Championships, where the Aggies finished 9th out of 11 teams with 503.5 points. Logan Brown paced the team with 67 individual points, including a 4th-place finish in the 200 breast (1:51.55).

Gee will arrive in fall 2028 as a member of the class of 2032, along with Lova Shteinberg, Dryden Finley, and David Davis. Davis is the #20 ranked recruit in the class.

For now, Gee keeps training with his club team, chasing faster times and bigger dreams.
why_it_matters: It shows how early top teenage athletes must make life-changing choices, and how a high school star's times are measured against a national standard, where even a fast swimmer can be several seconds away from the level needed to score at a major conference meet.

background_read: Texas A&M University (a large public university in College Station, Texas, whose sports teams are nicknamed the Aggies) competes in the SEC, the Southeastern Conference, one of the strongest leagues in American college sport.

In US college sport recruits often promise early: a 'verbal commitment' is a public announcement of where an athlete plans to go, but it is not binding until official papers are signed, so plans can still change.

St. Xavier High School (a Catholic boys' school in Cincinnati, Ohio) and the Cincinnati Marlins (a club team in the same city) are among Ohio's strongest swimming programmes, which is why Gee's times attract attention from big universities.

US college swimming is raced in short-course yards, in a 25-yard pool, rather than in the 50-metre Olympic pool, so the same event produces very different times: a 100-yard butterfly is swum roughly in the 44 to 46 second range, while the 100-metre version at the Olympics takes about 50 seconds.

Coaches have only a limited number of roster places and scholarships, so they compare a recruit's best times directly with what their current swimmers swim, which is exactly the comparison this article makes.

perspectives.description: Joining a Power-conference programme gives him elite coaching, training partners and a clear route towards bigger meets. The article's comparison shows he would already sit near A&M's top eight in two events, so he arrives with a real chance to score points.

Verbal commitments are not binding, and teenagers are asked to plan their futures years in advance while still growing and improving. There is also the personal cost of moving far from family in Ohio at seventeen or eighteen, with heavy training and academic demands.

US college swimming is a major pipeline towards the Olympics, but the gaps in this article show how deep the SEC is: times that win state titles are not always fast enough to final at a conference championship. The numbers also look different because college races are in yards, not Olympic metres.

Between now and 2028 the question is how much time Gee can drop, since SEC finals demanded 46.48 in the 100 fly and 1:44.80 in the 200 fly. If he improves at the rate he showed at Summer Juniors, he could join A&M's scoring group; if not, he may spend his first years fighting for a relay spot.
